author: claude

patch.value: The fallback was added while the registry was returning 404s, to get a release out. That trade is wrong for a supply-chain artifact: an unattested publish is not a degraded success, it is a different artifact. Failing the job leaves main holding the prepared version so the next run resumes the same release rather than inventing another one, which is exactly what the surrounding transaction was designed to do. pm-changelog already refuses; this converges the rest of the fleet onto that contract.
A failed provenance publish silently falls back to an unattested one

After three failed provenance publish attempts the release step called npm publish without --provenance and reported success. The only signal was a GitHub warning annotation. A transient registry failure therefore downgrades the package's supply-chain attestation permanently for that version, and consumers cannot tell an unattested publish caused by a 404 storm apart from one that never had provenance at all.

The release step has no publish path that omits --provenance; three provenance attempts are made; a version that landed despite a reported error is reconciled instead of republished; exhausting the attempts fails the job rather than publishing unattested; the workflow YAML parses and every bash run script passes bash -n.

value.author: claude
value.text: Reached only after three failed provenance attempts,which is precisely the state the fleet has been in since 2026-08-17. The first successful publish after the outage would have been the unattested one.

value.author: claude
value.text: Audited across the fleet: 17 of 18 published packages carried the identical fallback; only pm-changelog refused. The block was byte-identical in 16 of them.

value.author: claude
value.text: A fallback that weakens a security property is not a resilience measure. When the strong path fails,the correct outcome is no artifact,not a weaker artifact that looks the same to consumers.

value.note: publish step refuses to downgrade attestation and reconciles a late-landing version

author: claude

patch.value: The publish step drops the unattested fallback and converges on pm-changelog's contract: three attested attempts, a reconcile read for a version that landed despite a reported error, then a failing job. A new verify:release-publish-attestation gate finds every npm publish this repository can run and requires --provenance on each; it is wired into release:check and into CI as its own step.
No publish path omits --provenance, and a regression that reintroduces one fails a gate rather than shipping an unattested artifact.

Restoring the fallback makes the gate exit 1 naming the command; removing it again exits 0. Gates: typecheck 0, docstring 0 (8 files, 110 declarations), coverage 100/100/100/100 across 8 files, verify:release-changelog-date 0, verify:release-publish-attestation 0, 18 new tests pass.

message: Refuse to downgrade supply-chain attestation, and gate it

value.author: claude
value.text: Greptile round 1, both findings accepted and fixed. P2 (security): the gate tested for the --provenance SUBSTRING, so --provenance=false and --no-provenance both read as attested - the exact regression it exists to catch. attestationEnabled now tokenises and resolves last-flag-wins the way npm does. P1: with no sleep after the final attempt, the single reconcile read raced registry propagation and could fail a release npm had already accepted, skipping the tag and the GitHub release; it now polls three times with a 15s gap.

value.author: claude
value.text: Greptile round 2: the reconcile window I added was 30s, but this same workflow's bun verification step documents that the npm registry can take ~60s to propagate and gives itself 5 attempts at 30s. A shorter window here would fail a release that the very next step would then find. Widened to the same 5 attempts at 30s, deliberately matching that step's shape and numbers since it reads the same registry for the same version. Paid only on the path where npm already reported an error.

value.author: claude
value.text: CI caught a maintenance point the local run had half-hidden: the coverage-gate meta-tests enumerate this package's source files by hand in THREE places - one lcov fixture in 'defaults to its package root', and two more inside the fake npx script in 'direct entrypoint', one per platform. Adding a source file requires editing all three or the gate correctly reports it as never loaded. Updated all three.

value.author: claude
value.text: CodeRabbit full-review round: four findings, all acted on. (1) The recorded verification command was 'python3 scripts/verify-release-publish-attestation.ts' - the file is TypeScript run by node, so the receipt could never have run the gate. Replaced with the two commands that do run, and confirmed both exit 0 as recorded. (2) Major: every reconcile read tested 'npm view <pkg>@<ver> version', which proves only that the coordinate is occupied - not that the artifact is attested or came from this commit. All three reconcile points now require dist.attestations and refuse an unattested coordinate loudly rather than tagging around it. (3) The reconciliation window was already widened to 5 attempts at 30s in an earlier push. (4) stripQuotedSpans erased package.json script bodies, so a publish moved into an npm script was invisible to the gate; manifests are now expanded to their script command lines first.

value.author: claude
value.text: Greptile round 3: the scan required 'publish' to follow 'npm' immediately, so a real unattested publish written as 'npm --access public publish --ignore-scripts' was discarded before its flags were read, and an attested sibling elsewhere in the file carried the audit to a pass. isPublishCommand now tokenises and accepts publish anywhere after npm, excluding 'npm run publish' and 'npm run-script publish' because those run a package script whose body the manifest scan already covers. Found a second defect while fixing it: the line-level prefilter carried the same adjacency requirement, so widening only the judgement changed nothing - a prefilter must be at least as permissive as the judgement it feeds.

value.author: claude
value.text: Greptile round 4: reconcile_or_refuse called exit 1 from inside a helper the polling loop uses, so a version whose attestation metadata had not yet become visible - or a transient failure of that metadata read - terminated the step instead of being retried, skipping the tag and leaving npm ahead of Git. That is the exact split the release ordering exists to prevent, reintroduced by putting a decision inside a probe. Split into reconciled_attested, which only answers whether an attested copy is visible right now, and refuse_unattested_or_fail, reached only once the loop has stopped asking. Greptile also restated the artifact-identity gap that CodeRabbit raised: attestation presence does not bind the artifact to this commit. Acknowledged and still deferred - it needs the attestation bundle from dist.attestations.url, not a shell one-liner.

value.author: codex
value.text: Exact-head audit found a broader unresolved defect while dispositioning CodeRabbit's artifact-identity finding. npm audit signatures can cryptographically verify the exact downloaded package and expose its SLSA bundle,but the signed gitCommit is the workflow trigger SHA. Run 31993362652 and pm-ops@2026.8.17 both name 06b10d67169d17b2669c46becd33b9cb292c3bda even though that run merged release metadata and published from the later checkout. dist.attestations presence therefore does not establish the tagged commit. New critical blocker ops-xf9a owns the two-run release architecture and exact signed-statement validation; PR 65 must not merge until it is resolved and propagated.
